steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Intro
  - architecture simulation = cornerstone of designing/optimizing efficient computing systems
  - simulators like gem5: detailed insight into software/hardware microarchitecture interactions
  - but: big computational resources + time -> slows architectural exploration
  - our idea: augment simulators like gem5 with ML; ML model that mimics gem5's behavior
  - synergy of simulation + ML prediction
  - scenario: simulate app for brief interval, use that data to predict performance over longer periods
## Advancing Simulation with Machine Learning
  - ML already used for performance prediction in various contexts
  - inspired by approaches to improve simulator accuracy + efficiency
  - Renda et al.: integrating ML into architectural simulation
## Two Pathways to Machine Learning Integration
  - pathway 1: microarchitecture-independent app statistics
    - easy to get on real machines or fast functional simulators/emulators
    - e.g. instruction types in the code
    - models not influenced by microarchitecture; fast + versatile, but may miss hardware nuances
  - pathway 2: add microarchitectural features to the model
    - model learns impact of hardware-specific attributes
    - app stats + microarch features -> more comprehensive model of software/hardware interactions
## Our Research Objectives
  - main objective: model behavior of gem5 (well-established, versatile)
  - empower more detailed simulations with ML model -> faster simulation
  - give architects/researchers faster, more insightful way to study design choices + effect on app performance
  - rest of paper: methodology, experiments, results for both pathways
  - hope: future research with interplay of traditional simulation + ML prediction

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Computer architecture simulation is a cornerstone of designing and optimizing efficient computing systems. Simulators like gem5 have traditionally been very important because they give detailed insights into the complex interactions between software applications and hardware microarchitectures. But these simulations often need a lot of computational resources and time, and this limits how fast architectural exploration can go.

In this context, our research tries to augment traditional simulators like gem5 with machine learning. Our vision is to develop a machine learning model that mimics the behavior of gem5, so that users can use simulation and machine learning based prediction together. In this new paradigm, users would simulate an application for a short time interval and then use the simulation data from that to predict the performance of the application over longer time periods.

## Advancing Simulation with Machine Learning

Machine learning techniques have already been used for performance prediction in various contexts. Our work is inspired by similar approaches that tried to improve the accuracy and efficiency of simulators. For example, Renda et al. explored integrating machine learning techniques into architectural simulation and paved the way for this.

## Two Pathways to Machine Learning Integration
  - pathway 1: microarchitecture-independent app statistics
    - easy to get on real machines or fast functional simulators/emulators
    - e.g. instruction types in the code
    - models not influenced by microarchitecture; fast + versatile, but may miss hardware nuances
  - pathway 2: add microarchitectural features to the model
    - model learns impact of hardware-specific attributes
    - app stats + microarch features -> more comprehensive model of software/hardware interactions
## Our Research Objectives
  - main objective: model behavior of gem5 (well-established, versatile)
  - empower more detailed simulations with ML model -> faster simulation
  - give architects/researchers faster, more insightful way to study design choices + effect on app performance
  - rest of paper: methodology, experiments, results for both pathways
  - hope: future research with interplay of traditional simulation + ML prediction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Computer architecture simulation is a cornerstone of designing and optimizing efficient computing systems. Simulators like gem5 have traditionally been very important because they give detailed insights into the complex interactions between software applications and hardware microarchitectures. But these simulations often need a lot of computational resources and time, and this limits how fast architectural exploration can go.

In this context, our research tries to augment traditional simulators like gem5 with machine learning. Our vision is to develop a machine learning model that mimics the behavior of gem5, so that users can use simulation and machine learning based prediction together. In this new paradigm, users would simulate an application for a short time interval and then use the simulation data from that to predict the performance of the application over longer time periods.

## Advancing Simulation with Machine Learning

Machine learning techniques have already been used for performance prediction in various contexts. Our work is inspired by similar approaches that tried to improve the accuracy and efficiency of simulators. For example, Renda et al. explored integrating machine learning techniques into architectural simulation and paved the way for this.

## Two Pathways to Machine Learning Integration

The first pathway is about collecting application statistics that are microarchitecture-independent. These are easy to get on real machines or on functional simulators and emulators, which are known to be fast. The statistics include things like the types of instructions in the application code. If we train machine learning models on these features, we get models that are not influenced by microarchitectural details. However, these models might be fast and versatile, but they may not have the flexibility to account for the nuances of the underlying hardware.

The second pathway is to also include microarchitectural features in the machine learning model. With this approach the model can adapt and learn the nuanced impact of hardware-specific attributes. By using both application-specific statistics and microarchitectural features, we try to build a more comprehensive model that can capture the complex interactions between software and hardware.

## Our Research Objectives

Our main objective is to model the behavior of gem5, which is a well-established and versatile architectural simulator. Our vision is to make more detailed simulations possible by integrating a machine learning model, which accelerates the simulation process. If we achieve this, architects and researchers will have a faster and more insightful way to investigate different design choices and how they affect application performance.

In the next sections of this paper, we go through the methodology, experiments, and results of our exploration of these two machine learning integration pathways. With this empirical evidence, we hope to pave the way for future computer architecture simulation research, where traditional simulation and machine learning-enhanced prediction work together.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Computer architecture simulation is a cornerstone in the quest to design and optimize efficient computing systems [1]. Traditionally, simulators like gem5 [2] have been instrumental in providing detailed insights into the intricate interactions between software applications and hardware microarchitectures. However, these simulations often demand significant computational resources and time, which constrains the pace of architectural exploration.

In this context, our research seeks to augment traditional simulators like gem5 with machine learning. Our vision is to develop a machine learning model that mimics gem5's behavior, allowing users to harness the synergy between simulation and machine learning based prediction. In this paradigm, users simulate an application for a brief time interval and use the resulting simulation data to predict the application's performance over longer time periods.

## 1.1. Advancing Simulation with Machine Learning

Machine learning techniques have already been used for performance prediction in various contexts [3,4,5]. Our work is inspired by similar approaches that have sought to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of simulators. Renda et al. [6], for instance, paved the way by exploring the integration of machine learning techniques into architectural simulation.

## 1.2. Two Pathways to Machine Learning Integration

The first pathway centers on collecting application statistics that are microarchitecture-independent and readily obtainable on real machines or on functional simulators and emulators, which are known for their speed. These statistics include characteristics such as the types of instructions within the application code. By training machine learning models on these features, we can create models that are not influenced by microarchitectural details. However, such models, while potentially fast and versatile, may lack the flexibility to account for the nuances of the underlying hardware.

The second pathway incorporates microarchitectural features into the machine learning model. This gives the model the capability to adapt and learn the nuanced impact of hardware-specific attributes. By considering both application-specific statistics and microarchitectural features, we aim to construct a more comprehensive model that can capture the complex interactions between software and hardware.

## 1.3. Our Research Objectives

Our primary objective is to model the behavior of gem5, a well-established and versatile architectural simulator. Our vision is to empower more detailed simulations by integrating a machine learning model, thus accelerating the simulation process. By achieving this goal, we aim to offer architects and researchers a faster and more insightful means of investigating various design choices and their implications on application performance.

In the following sections of this paper, we describe the methodology, experiments, and results of our exploration of these two machine learning integration pathways. Through empirical evidence, we hope to pave the way for future computer architecture simulation research, marked by a harmonious interplay between traditional simulation and machine learning-enhanced prediction.
